# tstorch feature status report

Regenerate with `scripts/benchmark/benchmark-feature.sh --match <domain>`. Numbers here are parsed straight from pytest/pytest-benchmark JSON output - never hand-typed.

## Performance summary

How many features tstorch beats tsfresh on, per comparison category (mean vs. mean; only features with both a `tsfresh` and the given tstorch backend's recorded mean count toward that row. Rows without a native tsfresh axis borrow their matching real tsfresh row at render time, including the same-count row 7 tsfresh value for row 8 batched-argument variants). GPU counts are frequently noise-dominated for the single-trajectory variant specifically (tiny per-call kernel-launch overhead dominates real compute there) - read the per-feature tables' min/max before treating a single-trajectory GPU comparison as decisive.

| variant | tstorch_cpu faster | tstorch_cpu slower | tstorch_gpu faster | tstorch_gpu slower |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| single trajectory, direct_call, uncompiled | 35 | 36 | 16 | 55 |
| single trajectory, direct_call, **compiled** | 51 | 20 | 55 | 16 |
| 10,000 traj., tstorch direct_call uncompiled / tsfresh proxy_call | 71 | 0 | 71 | 0 |
| 10,000 traj., proxy_call, **compiled** (cold run) | 65 | 6 | 66 | 5 |

## Trajectory data

Single-trajectory and numerical-accuracy rows use `benchmarks/tstorch/cache/canonical_supervised_bounded.pt` - four of pybasin's own case-study ODE systems (`case_studies/pendulum`, `case_studies/duffing_oscillator`, `case_studies/lorenz`, `case_studies/friction`; exact params/initial conditions in `packages/tstorch/tests/utils/trajectory_builders.py::build_canonical_trajectories`), each integrated and filtered to its steady-state window:

| case | trajectories | states | T |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pendulum` | 2 | 2 | 50 |
| `duffing` | 5 | 2 | 5000 |
| `lorenz` | 2 | 3 | 4000 |
| `friction` | 2 | 2 | 500 |

Deliberately varied shapes/series lengths, including a very short one (`pendulum`), so a performance rewrite is checked for correctness (and numerical stability) across more than one regime. Same data backs both the numerical-accuracy and single-trajectory performance rows, so a rewrite is checked for correctness against the exact data it's benchmarked on.

10,000-trajectory rows use `benchmarks/tstorch/cache/pendulum_grid_10000.pt` - 10,000 `pendulum` trajectories (same ODE system/params as the canonical `pendulum` case above) sampled on a grid over initial conditions via `pybasin.sampler.GridSampler`, for batched-extractor-scale timing (see `trajectory_builders.py::build_pendulum_grid_trajectories`).

## Reading the tables

`tstorch_cpu`/`tstorch_gpu` "compiled (cold run)" rows are `[1]` round on purpose, not under-sampled: `torch.compile` caches compiled kernels by code structure + shape guards, not by object identity, so a second in-process "fresh extractor" call silently hits that cache instead of measuring a second genuine cold compile.

Numerical accuracy passes when `abs(diff) <= atol + rtol * abs(tsfresh)` and NaN positions match. The default tolerance is `atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-4`; feature rows show `-` for `atol` or `rtol` when that value uses the default.

## `approximate_entropy`

**Note:** tsfresh flags this `high_comp_cost=True` and excludes it from `EfficientFCParameters` - it's an O(T^2) all-pairs Chebyshev-distance comparison, called once *per* (m, r) combo (`fctype="simple"`), independently rebuilding the whole distance matrix each time and processing one series at a time. tstorch's `ApproximateEntropy.__call__` broadcasts all requested `(m, r)` combinations through running Chebyshev-distance passes and vectorizes every (B, S) series in the batch. This improves both parameter handling and per-series execution rather than merely porting the row-at-a-time implementation.

## `autocorrelation`

**Note:** tsfresh calls this once *per lag* (`fctype="simple"`) with no sharing between calls - every lag re-derives the series mean/variance from scratch. tstorch's `_autocorrelation_kernel` computes the shared autocovariance-vs-lag array once and reads every requested lag off of it, so batching lags here is a genuine algorithmic improvement over tsfresh's own approach, not just a faster port of the same computation. See references/api-design.md.

### Numerical accuracy vs. tsfresh

Test: `tests/unit/test_autocorrelation.py::test_autocorrelation_matches_tsfresh`

## `count_value`

**Note:** tsfresh calls `value_count` once per target value (`fctype="simple"`). tstorch broadcasts all requested values through one tensor comparison, including NaN matching, and avoids a Python-level call per parameter.

## `mean_n_absolute_max`

**Note:** tsfresh calls this once *per* `number_of_maxima` (`fctype="simple"`), independently re-sorting the absolute values each time. tstorch's `_mean_n_absolute_max` kernel sorts once (via `topk`) and reads a cumulative mean at every requested `number_of_maxima` off that one sort, so batching is a genuine algorithmic improvement over tsfresh's own approach.

## `number_cwt_peaks`

**Note:** tsfresh calls this once *per* n (`fctype="simple"`). tstorch places every requested Ricker width in one `conv1d` filter bank and shares that transform across n values. ## `number_peaks`

**Note:** tsfresh calls this once *per* n (`fctype="simple"`), independently rebuilding the rolled neighbour comparisons for that n each time. tstorch's `NumberPeaks` class unfolds once at the largest requested n and reads every smaller n's peak mask off a cumulative logical AND of the same comparisons (beating neighbours up to distance d implies beating them up to any smaller distance), so batching n's is a genuine algorithmic improvement over tsfresh's own approach, not just a faster port of the same per-n computation.

### Numerical accuracy vs. tsfresh

## `quantile`

**Note:** tsfresh calls this once *per* q (`fctype="simple"`), independently re-sorting the series each time. tstorch's `_quantile` kernel sorts once and reads every requested q off the same sorted series via linear interpolation, so batching q's is a genuine algorithmic improvement over tsfresh's own approach.

## `sample_entropy`

**Note:** tsfresh flags this `high_comp_cost=True` and excludes it from `EfficientFCParameters` - it's an O(T^2) all-pairs Chebyshev-distance comparison (`fctype="simple"`), processed one series at a time. `SampleEntropy.__call__` vectorizes that comparison across every (B, S) series in the batch. Since the feature has no parameters, the gain comes from per-series batching rather than parameter sharing.
